tagline.text: A pink-sand beach hidden on an island at Luzon's southern tip

image.credit: Maria Glenda Perico / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A beach on Calintaan Island off Matnog, the southernmost tip of Luzon, where white sand mixed with fragments of red coral gives it a soft pink tint. On this quiet, barely developed island you can swim, snorkel, and camp, then island-hop to Tikling Island and Huyog Lagoon.

Matnog is the southernmost town in Sorsogon province at the southeastern tip of Luzon, a port town where ferries cross the San Bernardino Strait to Samar. It sits at the Luzon end of the pan-Philippine highway (Maharlika Highway) that runs on to the Visayas and Mindanao, so large buses and trucks constantly load onto ferries here — yet just
20–30 minutes
out from the port by boat, an entirely different scenery opens up.

Subic Beach lies on the edge of Calintaan Island offshore from Matnog. Fine white sand mixed with fragments of red organ pipe coral gives the sand a soft pink hue, most visible in the early morning and evening when the sun sits low. The water is a clear jade in the shallows, deepening to blue farther out, and palm trees and green hills line the shore behind the beach.

The beach splits into two sections: the wider, more-visited "Subic Laki," and the quieter, more intimate "Subic Lijit." With almost no resort development — just a handful of nipa huts and a camping area — it suits travelers who prefer an island left in its natural state over one full of amenities. Boats can only be hired and visitors registered through the Matnog Tourism Office, which helps keep the island relatively clean.

The typical day trip pairs this with island hopping to Tikling Island, which has similarly pink-tinted sand, and Huyog Lagoon, a protected fish sanctuary. It also works well as a stop midway through a Sorsogon trip combined with Bulusan Lake and Donsol, or as a rest point on an overland Luzon–Visayas journey that continues by boat to Samar.

Get close to the beach and scoop up a handful of sand, and you'll see grains of red coral mixed into the white. The pink tint shows up more clearly in the early morning and late afternoon than under the harsh midday sun.

The water near shore is shallow and clear, great for swimming, while the rocky and coral edges are good for snorkeling among small tropical fish. Bring your own gear or check with the tourism office or boatmen about rentals.
A small island near Subic Beach, also known for its fine pinkish sand and clear water. It's usually included on the island-hopping route and tends to be quieter than Subic.
A lagoon connected to the sea where fish are raised and protected inside a pen. You can feed the fish (about
per boat) or snorkel among the shoals (about
per person). Sunscreen is banned here to protect marine life.
A clear-bottomed crystal kayak (about
for 30 minutes) lets you look down at the sandy bottom and coral from the water, which also makes for great photos. Check on site whether it's running.

Subic Laki has nipa huts and a camping area where you can pitch a tent and stay the night. The quiet beach after the day-trippers leave, the stars overhead, and the pink sand at first light are privileges reserved for overnight visitors.

blocks.title: Spotting Mount Bulusan Across the Water

children.text: On clear days, you can see the peak of Mount Bulusan to the north from the beach and out on the water. The view of the volcano and islands from the boat during island hopping is striking.

The island has limited electricity and drinking water, so bring a power bank, flashlight, and plenty of water, and carry all your trash back out.
Buses to Matnog or on to Samar and Leyte run daily from Manila's Cubao and PITX terminals, passing through Matnog port and loading onto the ferry. The trip to Matnog takes about
12–15 hours
, with fares around
depending on class. Be sure to tell the ticket seller you're getting off at Matnog.
A minibus or van from the Sorsogon City terminal to Matnog takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours

From Manila to Bicol International Airport (DRP) takes about
1 hour
, with one-way fares around
. From the airport, go to Legazpi Grand Central Terminal and take a bus to Matnog, or transfer in Sorsogon City. From Legazpi to Matnog is about
3–4 hours
by car.
Boats to Subic Beach are hired after registering at the Matnog Tourism Office (
). The tourism and environmental fee runs around
per person, and foreigners may be charged a higher registration fee.
Boats hold up to 10 people and run about
for a day trip or about
for an overnight trip. If your group is small, ask the tourism office about sharing a boat with other travelers. The crossing from Matnog port to Subic Beach takes about
20–30 minutes
Boats may be cancelled if the waves run high, so it's safer to depart early in the morning. Fees and rules change often, so check the latest notices.
Ferries to Matnog run several times a day from Allen or San Isidro port in Northern Samar, taking about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
. It's a good stop on the way back to Luzon after visiting Samar, including Biri Island.
Subic Beach is best visited during
March–May
, when the sea is calmest and the water clearest. Waves in the San Bernardino Strait are low during this period, so boats run smoothly, and midday temperatures of around
are great for swimming.
During
November–February
, the northeast monsoon (Amihan) often kicks up rough waves in the strait, and southern Bicol sees frequent rain even in this period.
August–November
often brings typhoons that halt boat service, and vehicles bound for Samar can back up heavily at Matnog port.
During Holy Week and summer weekends in
April–May
, domestic Filipino travelers increase sharply, so boats and camping spots fill up fast. Visit on a weekday if you want a quiet beach.

Staying on the island means using a nipa hut or the camping area at Subic Laki. Electricity and water are limited, so bring a tent, sleeping bag, flashlight, and drinking water, and ask the tourism office in advance whether tent rentals are available. For a more comfortable bed, you can stay at an inn or lodge in Matnog town (about
a night) and visit as a day trip, or stay in Sorsogon City (about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by car), which has more options.
There are almost no restaurants on the island, so buy fish, squid, meat, rice, fruit, water, and ice at the Matnog public market before you go. Pay a boatman or islander a cooking fee (about

per meal) and they'll grill and cook your ingredients into fish and seafood dishes. Near the port in town there are simple Filipino home-style eateries, and you can also try Sorsogon's local kinunot and spicy Bicol Express.
The tourism office opens at
. Arrive early in the morning if you want to depart while the sea is calm.
Boats are rented in units of 10 people, so if your group is small, sharing with other travelers cuts the cost significantly.
Buy plenty of food, water, and ice at the Matnog market before heading out — these are hard to find on the island.
Sunscreen isn't allowed at Huyog Lagoon, so cover up with a rash guard and hat instead.
Cell signal on the island can be weak or unavailable depending on your carrier. Bring a power bank.
Don't take sand or coral fragments home. The pink sand is coral that has broken down and accumulated over a long time.
Matnog port gets crowded with vehicles headed to Samar, so confirm your bus drop-off point and the tourism office location in advance.
Minibuses back to Sorsogon City thin out in the late afternoon. Check the time of the last trip.
The San Bernardino Strait has strong currents and fast-changing weather. Don't board a boat if waves are high or there's a weather advisory, and always wear a life vest on board.
Currents can run fast at the edges of the beach and in deeper water. Swim only in shallow areas and don't venture out far alone.
Wear aqua shoes to avoid stepping on coral and sea urchins, and don't touch or step on the coral.
The island has little shade or drinking water. Watch for dehydration and heatstroke, and bring plenty of water.
When camping, build fires only in designated spots, and carry all your trash back out.
Boats are prone to cancellation during the
August–November
typhoon season and the
November–February
monsoon season, so build slack into your schedule.
